Two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction take a comma before the conjunction, and «but» supplies the contrast.

A comma alone leaves a comma splice; neither mark leaves a run-on.

distractorRationale.B: Produces a run-on sentence.
distractorRationale.C: Places the comma after the conjunction rather than before it.

stem: The set of measurements, together with the calibration record, ______ been stored in the same archive since 1974.
explanation:
The subject is «the set», which is singular; «together with the calibration record» is parenthetical and does not change its number.

So the verb is «has been stored».

distractorRationale.A: Plural, and gives «are been».

stem: Since the ferry service ended in 2003 ______ the island has been reachable only by air.
explanation:
«Since the ferry service ended in 2003» is a dependent clause opening the sentence, and such a clause is followed by a comma.

«Since» already carries the causal link, so «so» would double it.

distractorRationale.A: Doubles the link already carried by «since».
distractorRationale.B: Requires an independent clause on its left.
distractorRationale.D: Requires an independent clause on its left.

stem: Each of the four samples ______ a different concentration of the compound.
explanation:
«Each» is singular regardless of what follows it, so the verb is «contains».

The present tense suits a standing description of the samples.

distractorRationale.A: Plural and shifts to the present perfect.
distractorRationale.B: Agrees with «samples» rather than with «each».

stem: The exhibition reunites four canvases that have not hung together since 1912 ______ two from Oslo, one from Chicago, and one from a private collection in Kyoto.
explanation:
A complete independent clause is followed by a list that specifies the «four canvases», which is the announcing use of a colon.

A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, and a bare comma would bury the introduction among the list's own commas.

distractorRationale.B: Loses the introduction among the list's commas.
distractorRationale.C: Runs the list into the clause without punctuation.
distractorRationale.D: Must be followed by an independent clause.

stem: The fellowship asks applicants to state a question, to describe a method, and ______ a schedule that can be met.
explanation:
The first two items are infinitive phrases — «to state» and «to describe» — so the third must be an infinitive too.

«To propose» completes the parallel series.

distractorRationale.A: A clause cannot serve as the third item.
distractorRationale.C: A past-tense verb breaks the series.
distractorRationale.D: A gerund breaks the infinitive series.

stem: Stored upright in a sealed case for eleven years ______ the violin needed only a new set of strings.
explanation:
The opening participial phrase modifies «the violin» and must be set off from the main clause by a comma.

A semicolon or colon would require an independent clause before it, and the phrase is not one.

distractorRationale.A: Runs the modifier into the clause it modifies.
distractorRationale.B: Requires an independent clause before it.
distractorRationale.D: Requires an independent clause before it.

stem: The readings, which had been taken by two independent teams, ______ within half a percent of each other.
explanation:
The subject is «readings», which is plural; the intervening relative clause does not affect agreement.

The past tense matches «had been taken».

distractorRationale.A: Singular and present tense.
distractorRationale.B: Singular and shifts tense.
distractorRationale.C: Singular, agreeing with nothing in the sentence.

stem: The orchard is picked twice each autumn ______ the fruit on the sunward side ripens a fortnight before the rest.
explanation:
Both halves are independent clauses, and the second explains the first without a coordinating conjunction, so a semicolon joins them.

A colon announces a list or specification the first clause points toward; here the first clause is a complete statement the second simply explains. A bare comma would be a splice.

distractorRationale.B: Produces a run-on.
distractorRationale.D: The first clause does not set up an announcement.

stem: Neither of the two proposed routes ______ the requirements set out in the environmental assessment.
explanation:
«Neither» as a pronoun is singular, so it takes «satisfies»; «of the two proposed routes» is a prepositional phrase and does not govern the verb.

The present tense suits a standing fact about the routes.

distractorRationale.A: Plural and shifts to the present perfect.

stem: The paper's central claim ______ depends on a sample of eleven households.

choices.text: that rural incomes had doubled within a decade,
—that rural incomes had doubled within a decade
, that rural incomes had doubled within a decade,
, that rural incomes had doubled within a decade

explanation:
The clause naming the claim interrupts the subject «the paper's central claim» and its verb «depends», so it must be enclosed by a matching pair of marks — here commas on both sides.

A mark on one side only, or a dash that opens what nothing closes, leaves the subject cut off from its verb.

distractorRationale.A: Closes the interruption without opening it.
distractorRationale.B: Opens with a dash and never closes the interruption.
distractorRationale.D: Opens the interruption without closing it.

stem: Sealed in a tin and forgotten in a cellar for sixty years, ______

choices.text: a collector found the negatives in perfect condition.
it was clear that the negatives had survived in perfect condition.
finding the negatives showed they were in perfect condition.
the negatives were in perfect condition when a collector found them.

explanation:
An opening participial phrase must modify the subject of the main clause. What was sealed in a tin and forgotten is the negatives, so «the negatives» must be the subject.

The other options make the collector, an act of finding, or «it» the thing in the cellar.

distractorRationale.A: Says the collector was sealed in a tin.
distractorRationale.B: «It» has no antecedent that could have been in the cellar.
distractorRationale.C: Says the finding was sealed in a tin.

stem: The two printings differ in more than the date on the title page ______ the second restores a dedication the author had withdrawn, while the first preserves a preface she later disowned.
explanation:
The first clause makes a general statement, and what follows spells it out — the announcing use of a colon after a complete independent clause.

The second half already carries commas and a «while» clause, so a bare comma would blur the line between claim and elaboration.

distractorRationale.B: Produces a comma splice before a clause already heavy with commas.
distractorRationale.C: Coordination without a comma, and it obscures the explanatory relation.

stem: The registrar noted that the two ledgers, kept in different offices and by clerks who never met, ______ nonetheless identical in their totals.
explanation:
The subject is «the two ledgers», which is plural; the long modifier between subject and verb does not change that.

The past tense matches «noted» in the main clause.

distractorRationale.A: Singular, agreeing with none of the candidates for subject.
distractorRationale.D: Singular and shifts to the present perfect.
